title: Linked Lists
summary: A chain of nodes held together by pointers — the structure that teaches you to think in references, and the source of half of all easy/medium interview questions.

blocks.markdown:
A linked list is a chain of nodes, each pointing to the next — no contiguous memory required.

- A **node** holds a value plus a **pointer** to the next node; the list is just a reference to the first node, the **head**.
- Nodes are **scattered in memory**; the pointers are the only thing keeping the sequence in order.
- **Insert/delete at a known spot is O(1)** — rewire a pointer, no shifting.
- **Access by index is O(n)** — there's no address math; you walk from the head one node at a time.

blocks.subTitle: Three flavors
blocks.markdown:
Same idea, three wirings.

| Flavor | Each node points to |
|---|---|
| Singly | next only |
| Doubly | next and prev |
| Circular | last loops to head |

- **Doubly** lets you walk backward and detach a held node in O(1), at the cost of one extra pointer each.
- **Circular** is natural for round-robin and ring buffers — but a naive walk never terminates.

blocks.subTitle: Singly vs doubly
blocks.markdown:
A node is the atom: a value and one or two pointers.

![Singly versus doubly linked list nodes](assets/a06-linked-lists/singly-vs-doubly.svg)

- **Singly** — each node points forward via `next`; the chain ends at `null`. Walking is one-way and O(n).
- **Doubly** — each node also carries `prev`, so you move either way and detach a node in O(1) given only that node.
- A singly list must walk from the head to find a node's predecessor — that's why doubly wins for in-place deletes.

assets.alt: Singly versus doubly linked list nodes

blocks.subTitle: Core operations & costs
blocks.markdown:
Every edit is just a few pointer writes — but order matters.

- **Insert at head** — point the new node's `next` at the old head, then move `head`. O(1).
- **Insert after node `p`** — `new.next = p.next; p.next = new`. O(1). Flip the order and you lose the tail.
- **Delete `p`'s successor** — `p.next = p.next.next`. O(1).
- **Access index k / search** — walk from head. O(n).
- **Insert/delete at tail** — O(1) only if you keep a `tail` pointer, else O(n).

blocks.subTitle: Fast & slow pointers
blocks.markdown:
Run two pointers at different speeds — `slow` one node per step, `fast` two — and a lot falls out of a single pass.

- **Find the middle** — when `fast` hits the end, `slow` sits at the midpoint.
- **k-th from the end** — push `fast` ahead by `k`, then advance both; when `fast` ends, `slow` is the answer.
- **Detect a cycle** — if the two ever meet, the list loops.

All three are O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

blocks.subTitle: Floyd's cycle detection
blocks.markdown:
A cycle means some `next` loops back, so traversal never ends. Floyd's tortoise and hare catches it cheaply.

![Floyd fast and slow cycle detection](assets/a06-linked-lists/floyd-cycle.svg)

- No cycle → `fast` runs off the end and you stop.
- Cycle → `fast` keeps lapping the loop and **must** land on `slow`, like a fast runner lapping a slow one.
- O(n) time, **O(1) space** — no hash set needed.
- To find the cycle's start: after they meet, reset one pointer to `head` and step both together until they meet again.

assets.alt: Floyd fast and slow cycle detection

blocks.subTitle: In-place reversal
blocks.markdown:
Reverse a singly list by flipping every `next` backward in one walk, juggling three references.

![In-place reversal pointer rewiring](assets/a06-linked-lists/reversal.svg)

- `prev` starts `null`, `curr` at the head, and you **save** `next` before overwriting.
- Each step: stash `next = curr.next`, point `curr.next` back at `prev`, then slide both forward.
- When `curr` is `null`, `prev` is the new head.
- Skip the save and you orphan the rest of the list — the classic rewire bug.

blocks.subTitle: Cycle detection in code
blocks.markdown:
The tortoise-and-hare loop, end to end.

```python
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = fast = head
    while fast and fast.next:
        slow = slow.next        # one step
        fast = fast.next.next   # two steps
        if slow is fast:
            return True         # they met -> cycle
    return False                # fast fell off the end
```

- The `while fast and fast.next` guard is what lets `fast` safely take two steps.
- O(n) time, O(1) space.

blocks.subTitle: The dummy node trick
blocks.markdown:
A dummy node makes the "what if it's the head?" special case disappear.

- Create a throwaway node whose `next` points at the real head, then run your logic from the dummy.
- Now the head has a predecessor, so deleting or inserting before it is no longer a special case.
- Return `dummy.next` at the end as the new head.
- It removes a whole class of off-by-one and null bugs in merge, remove-Nth, and insert problems.

blocks.subTitle: List vs array
blocks.markdown:
They trade indexing for structural edits — and cache locality changes the real answer.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Fast access by index | Array |
| O(1) splice at held node | Linked list |
| Tight scans, speed matters | Array |
| Cheap merge of sequences | Linked list |

Arrays often win even for inserts: contiguous memory is far faster to scan than chasing scattered pointers. See [a02-arrays-strings](a02-arrays-strings.md).

blocks.subTitle: Why arrays usually win
blocks.markdown:
Big-O hides a brutal constant factor here.

- A cache hit costs roughly **1 ns**; a cache miss to main memory roughly **100 ns** — about 100x slower.
- Array scans read contiguous bytes, so the CPU **prefetches** and almost every read is a hit.
- A linked-list walk jumps to scattered addresses — almost every read can be a miss.
- Each node also pays at least one pointer (8 bytes) plus heap overhead, often more than the value itself.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
Where linked lists actually earn their keep.

- **LRU cache** — a **doubly linked list + hash map**: the map finds a node in O(1), the list orders by recency; move-to-front and tail-eviction are both O(1). See [b05-caching](b05-caching.md).
- **Linux kernel** — intrusive doubly-linked circular lists (`list_head`) for run/wait queues; cheap splicing, rarely indexed.
- **Allocators** — free blocks tracked as a list; free pushes O(1), allocate pops O(1).
- **Java `LinkedList` vs `ArrayList`** — `ArrayList` usually wins anyway; the cautionary tale.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"Lists beat arrays because insert is O(1)."** Traversal and cache misses dominate; arrays usually win.
- **Orphaning the tail.** Always save `curr.next` *before* you overwrite it.
- **Assuming the head never changes.** Delete-head, reverse, and insert-front need a dummy node or explicit handling.
- **Forgetting a pointer in a doubly list.** Every edit touches up to four pointers — write a checklist.
- **Thinking cycle detection needs a hash set.** Floyd's does it in O(1) space.
